The Rascals - People Got to Be Free (1968)

"People Got to Be Free" is a song released in 1968 by The Rascals. Written by group members Felix Cavaliere and Eddie Brigati and featuring a lead vocal from Cavaliere, it is a musically upbeat but impassioned plea for tolerance and freedom:

"All the world over, so easy to see! People everywhere, just wanna be free. Listen, please listen! that's the way it should be Peace in the valley, people got to be free."

In the song's coda, Felix says in a half-sung, half-spoken voice, that the "Train of Freedom", is "about to arrive any minute now", that "it has been long, long overdue", and that it's "coming right on through", before the song's fade with Felix saying "Chug" repeatedly. It became a big hit in the turbulent summer of 1968.

While "People Got to Be Free" was perceived by some as related to the assassinations of Martin Luther King, Jr. and Robert F. Kennedy earlier that year, it was recorded before the latter's death. In fact it was partly a reaction to an ugly encounter wherein the long-haired group was threatened by a group of strangers after their tour vehicle broke down in Fort Pierce, Florida.

The song is clearly a product of its times; however, two decades later writer Dave Marsh included it as number 237 in his book Heart of Rock and Soul: The 1001 Greatest Singles of All Time, saying in reference to, and paraphrase of, the song's lyric, "Ask me my opinion, my opinion will be: Dated, but NEVER out of date."

After this song came out, the Rascals would only perform at concerts that featured an African American act; if those conditions were not met, the Rascals canceled several shows in protest.

Without getting into the historical reasons that it was initially made illegal, there's a pretty simple reason why it's still illegal. All the things people have mentioned like it being rather inconvenient to pharmaceuticals and so on are true, but it's really a whole lot more simple. It's extremely easy to outlaw things, but really really hard to decriminalize things.

The reason is that when you want to reduce punishment on something you can be seen as not only condoning but even encouraging it. From a political point of view it's just a bad decision. Who are you going to please? The small few who genuinely believe in a small government and some people who stand to benefit from it. Who are you going to anger? Pretty much everybody that's conservative on social issues, religious folks, older folks (in general), and so on. The people you please don't vote and/or are unlilkely to change their vote based on this. The people you anger do vote and are likely to see this as a sharp blow against their beliefs.

This isn't unique to the US. I imagine this phenomena played a role in how Islam went from 'dress modestly' to 'cover yourself head to toe in a pitch black potato sack and don't you dare let an eyeball show.' A view for more modesty is seen as more pious. A view against it would be seen as degeneracy. We're having our issue with this today in terms of free speech. Allowing people to say despicable things is being framed as supporting what they're saying. It's a strong force to work against, and the reason that -for the most part- once something becomes illegal, it's likely to stay that way.

It's also the reason that, for instance, things like "hard on crime" that's led to skyrocketing prison populations for victimless crimes were so easy to sell. In reality a big part of those laws were complete corruption and private prisons lobbying to get more people in prison. And it's accomplished very little aside from resulting in us having more prisoners per capita than anywhere in the world (seriously - we have more prisoners per capita than even places like Russia and China) but it sounds good and moral and creates a hell of a strawman. Who are you going to vote for? The guy who's hard on crime or the guy who thinks we ought treat criminals better? Same issue with weed.
